strengths: Clearly identifies and empirically demonstrates two concrete failure modes of prior context-adaptation methods (brevity bias and context collapse), including a compelling case study (Figure 2) showing a sharp accuracy/token collapse in Dynamic Cheatsheet.

Broad and fairly rigorous empirical evaluation spanning offline (system prompt) and online (test-time memory) adaptation across agent (AppWorld) and domain-specific (FiNER, Formula) benchmarks, with consistent, sizable gains (10.6% agents, 8.6% finance) over multiple strong baselines (ICL, MIPROv2, GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet).

Practical significance is well supported: substantial reductions in rollouts, latency (up to ~91.5%), and dollar cost compared to GEPA/DC, plus a leaderboard comparison showing a smaller open-source model matching/surpassing a GPT-4.1-based production agent.
Good ablation study isolating the contribution of the Reflector, multi-epoch refinement, and offline warmup, supporting the claimed design choices.

High transparency/reproducibility effort: full prompts for Generator/Reflector/Curator and baselines are released in the appendix, and the method is described in enough detail (bullet metadata, delta updates, grow-and-refine) to reimplement.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: ACE is explicitly built on top of Dynamic Cheatsheet's agentic architecture, and the core new ideas (itemized bullets, delta updates, dedup via embeddings, separate reflector) are largely engineering refinements of existing memory/context frameworks (A-MEM, DC, GEPA) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation is limited to a single base LLM family (DeepSeek-V3.1) and a narrow domain-specific application (financial XBRL tasks); generality of the 'domain-specific benchmark' claims and robustness across different model scales/architectures is untested.

Results without ground-truth labels are inconsistent: in Table 2, ACE without GT/execution signals sometimes underperforms the base LLM (e.g., FiNER online -3.4), undercutting the abstract's claim that ACE 'could adapt effectively without labeled supervision,' which appears true mainly for agent tasks with rich execution feedback but not more generally.

No variance/multiple-seed reporting; all numbers appear to be single-run results, raising concerns about the statistical reliability of the reported gains, especially given the relatively small absolute differences in some ablations.

Comparison to baselines could be seen as somewhat asymmetric since ACE contexts are substantially longer (thousands of tokens) than the concise prompts produced by GEPA/MIPROv2 by design; while the paper argues long-context serving costs are amortized, no direct inference-time latency/cost comparison for using the resulting (longer) ACE context at serving time is provided, only adaptation-time costs.

The AppWorld leaderboard comparison is a moving-target, timestamped snapshot (Sept 2025) that may not be reproducible/verifiable by future readers, weakening the strength of this particular claim over time.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and well-illustrated problem (brevity bias and context collapse), with a concrete empirical demonstration (Figure 2) that grounds the paper's core claims.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple task types (agentic AppWorld, financial reasoning, medical reasoning, text-to-SQL) and multiple LLM backbones (DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, Llama-3.3-70B), showing the method generalizes across models and domains.
Strong and consistent performance gains over reasonably strong baselines (ICL, MIPROv2, GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet) in both offline and online adaptation settings.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of the Reflector, multi-epoch adaptation, incremental delta updates, and hyperparameter sensitivity (dedup threshold, pruning trigger, reflection iterations).
Practical, systems-level cost/latency analysis (rollouts, tokens, KV-cache reuse) that meaningfully addresses concerns about the practicality of long, evolving contexts.
Additional analyses on robustness to noisy/harmful reflection and weaker Reflector models strengthen the credibility of the approach's robustness claims.
Detailed prompts and experimental settings are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: ACE is explicitly built on top of Dynamic Cheatsheet's agentic architecture, and the main additions (separate Reflector role, delta updates, grow-and-refine merging) are largely engineering refinements rather than fundamentally new algorithmic ideas; overlap with existing agent-memory frameworks (A-MEM, AWM) is only briefly discussed.

Reported results appear to be from single runs without variance/multiple-seed reporting, which is concerning given the benchmarks (especially AppWorld) are known to be noisy; this makes it hard to assess the statistical significance of the reported gains.

The comparison against IBM CUGA on the AppWorld leaderboard is prominently featured in the abstract/intro as a headline result, but the paper itself caveats that it is not a controlled, apples-to-apples comparison (different agent architectures, tools, and models), creating some tension between the marketing framing and the acknowledged limitations.

The central thesis that 'more comprehensive, longer contexts are better' is contradicted by the paper's own discussion (e.g., HotpotQA, Game of 24 needing concise contexts), suggesting the generality of the claimed insight is narrower than implied by the abstract.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is only partially addressed: ACE consumes substantially more input tokens at evaluation time than GEPA baselines, and while KV-cache reuse arguments are offered to mitigate this, actual cost may vary substantially depending on deployment/serving infrastructure and is not universally guaranteed.

The offline ACE variant with ground-truth labels is compared to GEPA/MIPROv2 also using labels, but the framing sometimes conflates label-free and label-based results, which could confuse readers about when ACE truly operates without supervision.

No systematic study of how the accumulated playbook scales or degrades over very long adaptation horizons (beyond the 80-step case study), nor a human evaluation of the claimed interpretability of the resulting bulleted playbooks.

strengths: Clearly identifies and empirically demonstrates two real problems in context adaptation (brevity bias and context collapse), with a compelling illustrative case study (Figure 2) showing sudden context collapse on AppWorld.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark families (AppWorld agent tasks, financial reasoning FiNER/Formula, plus medical DDXPlus and text-to-SQL BIRD-SQL) and multiple LLM backbones (DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, Llama-3.3-70B), showing fairly consistent relative gains.

Thorough ablation and sensitivity analyses (Reflector necessity, multi-epoch adaptation, incremental vs. monolithic updates, reflection iteration count, deduplication threshold, pruning trigger, robustness to weak/adversarial reflectors) that help substantiate the design choices.

Practically useful cost/latency analysis showing large reductions in rollouts, latency, and token cost relative to GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet, plus a reasonable discussion of KV-cache amortization for longer contexts.
Transparent discussion of limitations, including dependence on reflector/feedback quality and settings where rich contexts are unnecessary.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core architecture is explicitly built on top of Dynamic Cheatsheet (Generator/Reflector/Curator plus delta updates), and GEPA-style reflective updates already exist; the main contribution is largely an engineering refinement (itemized bullets + incremental merge) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The headline claim of self-improvement 'without labeled supervision' is undercut by the paper's own results: Table 2 shows ACE (and DC) can substantially degrade below the base LLM when ground-truth/execution signals are unreliable (e.g., FiNER online without GT drops to 67.3, -3.4), which is a significant caveat that is somewhat downplayed in the abstract/intro relative to how prominently the unsupervised claim is advertised.

No variance/multiple-run reporting or statistical significance testing is provided anywhere in the paper; given some of the reported swings (e.g., large accuracy differences between adjacent hyperparameter settings, or between GT/no-GT online settings), it is hard to assess whether reported gains are robust or partly due to run-to-run noise.

The prominent comparison to the AppWorld leaderboard's top entry (IBM CUGA) is used rhetorically in the abstract and introduction to claim 'matches/surpasses' a production system, but is heavily caveated in a footnote as not a controlled methodological comparison — this framing risks overstating practical significance.

Baseline fairness is somewhat asymmetric: GEPA/MIPROv2/ICL are only evaluated with ground-truth labels while ACE is evaluated both with and without, and DSPy baselines are run with a single 'auto=heavy' configuration without deeper tuning discussion, which could bias comparisons in ACE's favor.

Core algorithmic details of the 'grow-and-refine' de-duplication (embedding-based similarity, thresholds, when pruning triggers) are relegated to the appendix and are only lightly specified in the main text, limiting a reader's ability to fully judge or reproduce this design choice from the main paper alone.

The method uses the same strong LLM for Generator/Reflector/Curator, tripling inference calls per adaptation step; while rollout/latency numbers are reported, the practical deployment overhead of running three LLM roles is not deeply analyzed relative to simpler single-call baselines beyond the specific cost tables shown.

strengths: Clearly identifies and empirically demonstrates two concrete failure modes in existing context-adaptation methods (brevity bias and context collapse), with a compelling case study (Figure 2) showing dramatic performance drop from context collapse.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning agentic (AppWorld) and domain-specific (FiNER, Formula, plus DDXPlus and BIRD-SQL in appendix) benchmarks, in both offline and online adaptation settings, with consistent and often large gains over strong baselines (ICL, MIPROv2, GEPA, Dynamic Cheatsheet).

Strong ablation and sensitivity analyses: isolating the contribution of the Reflector, multi-epoch adaptation, offline warmup, and incremental delta updates; robustness tests under weak or adversarially harmful reflectors; hyperparameter sensitivity across reflection iterations, dedup threshold, and pruning triggers.

Thorough cost/latency analysis (rollouts, tokens, dollar cost) showing ACE is not only more accurate but also substantially cheaper and faster than GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet, and a thoughtful discussion of KV-cache reuse mitigating the cost of longer contexts.
Generalization experiments across four different LLM backbones (DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-5.1, Llama-3.3-70B) show the method is not backbone-specific.

Practically relevant result: matching/exceeding a production-level agent (IBM CUGA) on a public leaderboard using a smaller open-source model, with an appropriately hedged claim about this comparison.
Good reproducibility support: detailed prompts for Generator/Reflector/Curator are provided in the appendix, and the method is described with sufficient implementation detail.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to Dynamic Cheatsheet and other memory-augmented agent frameworks (A-MEM, AWM); the core contribution is largely the addition of a separate Reflector role, itemized delta updates, and grow-and-refine deduplication rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

The comparison against GEPA/MIPROv2/DC may be confounded by context length and total inference-time compute: ACE's context playbooks are often much larger (richer prompts), which could partly explain gains independent of the specific architectural design; a controlled comparison matching total token/compute budget would strengthen the claims.

Feedback-quality dependency is a real and somewhat impactful limitation: without ground-truth labels or reliable execution signals, both ACE and DC degrade (sometimes below baseline) on the finance benchmarks, indicating the method's benefits are contingent on the availability of good feedback signals, which may not always be present in practice.

The AppWorld leaderboard comparison to IBM CUGA, while interesting, is explicitly caveated by the authors as not a rigorous methodological comparison (different agent designs, potentially different tooling), which somewhat weakens the headline claim in the abstract.

The grow-and-refine deduplication step (embedding-based semantic merging) is not deeply analyzed for potential loss of valid diverse insights or increased latency at scale as playbooks grow very large over long deployments.

Domain-specific evaluation is somewhat narrow in the main text (finance-focused), with medical/SQL results relegated to a brief appendix mention, limiting the ability to assess generalization depth from the main narrative.

Limited exploration of failure cases beyond the adversarial-reflector experiment; it would be useful to see more analysis of scenarios where ACE's assumption (that LLMs benefit from long, itemized contexts rather than compressed ones) breaks down in practice beyond the brief discussion in §5.
